item.content:encoded:
I use AI for writing all the time. But not because it’s good at writing.

In fact, just the opposite is true. AI is so reliably bad at writing that I’ve actually taken advantage of that, and made its bad writing an integral part of my writing process.

I’ve written a lot of books and articles over the years, and while I used to start with an outline, I don’t anymore. These days I do a lot of brain dumping and brainstorming and talking out loud to an AI, working out what I think about something. I accumulate a lot of notes and ideas, and run a lot of experiments, and at some point, if I’m lucky, I decide there might be an article somewhere in all of that.

Then I ask the AI to take everything I’ve given it and write a draft.

And that AI-generated draft is universally terrible. Like, some of the worst writing you can imagine.

Which is exactly what I want.

Instead of an outline, I get an entire “article” or “chapter” (or, at least, a weird facsimile of one), with paragraphs that express complete thoughts that I gave the AI. Granted, those paragraphs are full of obvious AI tics, like how it uses em dashes to squish two unrelated sentences together, or weird staccato sentences one after another, or these insufferable parades of sentence fragments. Maybe the worst tic is that half of the paragraphs AI generates have an extra sentence that doesn’t actually say anything, but just delivers a forced conclusion with fake “punchiness.” I guess maybe AIs were trained on a lot of bad writing? Well, whatever, it works for me.

The reason I love that type of obviously bad AI writing is because when I’m looking at one of its paragraphs, it’s immediately obvious that an AI wrote it. I’ve been thinking of it as a kind of an improved “lorem ipsum” that lets me see how my article will look, while still serving as a functional placeholder. That lets me use it the way I would use an outline: I can move parts of the article around, make sure it flows correctly, and then replace ALL of the bad AI writing with (hopefully) decent human writing, just like I used to do with bullets in my old outlines.

One weird side-effect of writing this way is that it’s made me very sensitive to the different kinds of AI tics and tells. And I think the weirdest and most frustrating one is “Yoda-speak,” where the AI literally talks like Yoda. It’s weird, kind of hilarious, annoying, and pervasive, but most of all, it’s fascinating. Why does the AI keep talking like Yoda? What causes it? Can we do anything about it? (Do we even want to? It certainly makes it easy to identify AI-generated text, and also, it’s often unintentionally hilarious.)

I’ve got a theory about why this happens, and I ran an experiment that generated some evidence to support it. But first… what, exactly, is Yoda-speak?

Backwards, this bad writing is

I’ve been working on my latest book. It’s called Be the Model, and it teaches you how LLMs work by having you build interactive pages that let you literally do the job of a model to get an intuitive understanding of how they work. So I’ve been writing a lot, which means I’ve been confronted with a lot of Yoda-speak.

Here’s a great example from the chapter I’m currently working on (the “pond sentences” are a small training text), from a description of a page that you’ll build to learn how training works:

The eight pond sentences fill the left region, every word clickable.

That’s weird, right? Nobody talks like that.

To be perfectly fair, I’ll need you to suspend your disbelief a little. Yoda would probably say something more like, “The left region, filled by the eight pond sentences is. Clickable, every word must be.” But the AI-generated version is still very weird, and in a pattern that is recognizably Yoda-like.

That’s a pattern I’ve seen a lot. At one point I was looking through some AI-generated text, trying to figure out a particularly unintelligible sentence. When I asked Claude Opus for help, it came up with the term “Yoda-speak,” and I’ve since found that using that term is really useful when trying to get an AI to help decipher sentences like that.

The interesting thing is that AIs are perfectly capable of detecting and correcting Yoda-speak. You can try this yourself: start a new ChatGPT session, paste in that “pond” sentence, tell it: “An AI generated that sentence. That’s Yoda-speak.” I just tried that in an incognito window, and here’s the answer it just gave me:

Yep —that’s unmistakably Yoda-speak. A natural version would be:

“The eight pond sentences fill the left region, with every word being clickable.”

Or, more naturally for UI instructions:

“The left region contains the eight pond sentences, and every word is clickable.”

The original sounds like the AI took normal English, rearranged the syntax, and then forgot to put it back.

This particularly ugly sentence, from one of those AI-generated outlines of a later chapter that I haven’t started writing yet about the attention mechanism (the part of the LLM that understands context and relationships between words), is the example that made me want to write this article:

What’s left is to let the two heads’ work combine, so run the combined eight numbers through one more small table, eight in and eight out, square, called the output projection.

Ugh.

The problem with that sentence, and what made it hard to diagnose what was going on, is that when you first look at it you can basically understand what it’s saying (sort of?), and it’s hard to put your finger on exactly what’s wrong with it. It’s obviously terrible writing, but that’s not unique. AI is a universally awful writer.

What’s uniquely wrong with that sentence is its weird, comma-laden structure. Different parts of the sentence are split up into small comma-separated phrases, and AIs seem especially prone to using them to rearrange sentences, often at the expense of readability. That particular sentence is about running a combined set of eight numbers through one additional small 8×8 table. But the part of the sentence that should have described the table was in the second half of the sentence, and then you learn at the very end that the whole thing is called an output projection (but only after you’ve already been told to run numbers through it). Somehow the components of the sentence were arranged in a way that made it almost unintelligible.

One word at a time, it writes

An LLM is a next-word predictor. It works by taking your prompt, all of the context you’ve fed it, and everything it’s generated so far, generating the next word in its response, and then repeating the whole process for the next word, then the next one, and so on. It’s counterintuitive to think that AIs could possibly work that way, because these things can produce long, complex, and generally coherent and helpful responses. It seems very strange that they do all of that work one word at a time, without following a master plan for a response.

But that’s literally how the AI works. Once an LLM generates a word, it’s part of the response. It generally can’t go back and rearrange the first half of a sentence, even though it hasn’t finished generating it.

And that brings me back to that especially weird “eight in and eight out, square” barely intelligible sentence. Here’s what I think happened. The model generated the sentence up through “run the combined eight numbers through one more small table,” so those words were already baked into the response. Then it figured out that it had three more things it wanted to say about that table. But by that time it was too late to go back and put those details where they belonged, and apparently there was a shortage of periods that week, or possibly a surplus of commas (there’s no way to know for sure), so it just smashed each of those thoughts onto the end of an already awkward sentence.

I did some research to try to figure out if anyone has looked into this phenomenon before. The closest thing I found to an answer is a 2024 paper by Wilson Wu, John X. Morris, and Lionel Levine called “Do language models plan ahead for future tokens?” They were attempting to determine whether a model does real advance work for words it hasn’t written yet, or whether the information that pays off later is a byproduct of whatever was useful at the time.

The experiment that Wu et al. did was actually pretty clever. In normal training, when the model is being corrected for mispredicting a word several steps ahead, that correction reaches back and shapes what it computed at earlier positions. That way, the model learns to prepare information at an early word for the benefit of words further along, which is the “planning ahead” the paper is testing for. So they trained one model normally, and a second one with a modified process that cut that out: each position could only be trained to help predict the very next word. They kept next-word prediction but removed the training signal from words two or more steps ahead.

Then the researchers compared how well the two models predicted text: if the normally trained model did better, that would be evidence that preparing information in advance was actually helping. With ordinary language, the difference was fairly small for GPT-2, although it became larger as they tested bigger models.

So there’s evidence that a model can sometimes prepare information that will be useful later, which means my story about it only figuring things out as it goes is probably too simple. But anticipating is not revising. Whatever the model sees coming, it still can’t reach back and reorder the words it already committed to, and the words it already committed to are where the damage shows up.

Better, the second answer often is

I have a theory that the Yoda-speak phenomenon is closely related to something I see all the time (and I expect you do, too). Say you’re asking an AI for help with an email, and it gives you a draft of a sentence. Then, immediately after it gives you that sentence, it says something like this: “A better way to phrase that would be:” and gives you a second version. Sometimes there’s even a third option. And it almost always tells you it prefers the last one that it generated.

Coincidentally, I ran into a good example of that “here’s a better version” phenomenon when I asked ChatGPT to make the pond sentence more Yoda-like. I literally gave it the prompt make it more yoda-like. Here’s what it said:

More Yoda-like

The left region, the eight pond sentences fill. Clickable, every word is.

Or even more Yoda:

Extra Yoda-like

The left region, filled by the eight pond sentences is. Clickable, every word must be.

At this point, you can probably guess what I think happened. It generated the first version, and now that version was part of the context it had to work with. Then it generated a second version that was even more Yoda-like. But the first version was already there, so it couldn’t replace it. All it could do was give me another one. I see AIs do this kind of self-correction all the time.

If that’s what’s happening, then self-correction and Yoda-speak may be two versions of the same basic limitation. The model can’t go back and change what it already wrote. Sometimes that means the better answer comes afterward. Other times it means a thought that belonged earlier gets smashed onto the end of a sentence.

My own experiment, I ran

After looking at these two related phenomena (the AI generating Yoda-speak and constantly generating a second or even a third option), I got thinking. I started to wonder if this wasn’t just an AI fluke but actually something that I could reproduce and even potentially control. It would be really interesting if the way we give facts to the AI and structure the input could actually have an outsized effect on how it generates its output, especially if seemingly innocuous changes could cause it to create really weird results.

This was a real experiment, because this approach isn’t obviously something that should work. In theory, if you give a model a set of facts, it should be able to produce coherent output no matter how you order those facts. But I’ve been looking at how attention works in LLMs lately because I need to explain it for Be the Model in straightforward terms that anyone can understand. It seemed to me that changing the order of the facts could actually change what the model was paying attention to.

It turns out that there are two different mechanisms at work inside the LLM, and my theory was that they each played a part in both phenomena, the Yoda-speak and the unprompted second answers:

  • Attention is about what the model is looking at in the input. Every time the AI generates a new word, it looks back over the whole prompt and everything it has written so far, and weights the parts differently depending on their content and their shape. That weighting is a big part of what makes it good at predicting the next word. I had a theory that three facts written as complete sentences would get interpreted as facts to reorganize, while the same exact facts written as bare fragments might look like pieces that could be pasted right after a noun, and attention would weight them that way and send the model down a bad path.
  • Autoregression is about what the model has already written. The AI is a “predict the next word” machine: it generates one word at a time, and each of those words becomes part of what it’s looking at when it picks the next one. Once it’s written one more small table, it can’t go back and insert square before table, so if any facts about the table are still unexpressed at that moment, the only place left for them is later in the sentence. If attention had already sent the model down a bad path, autoregression would keep it from repairing the opening.

My guess was that the “I prefer the second answer” text that the AI keeps generating is essentially a mechanism for recovering from weird phrasing, and that the Yoda-speak or other weird phrasing was the underlying phenomenon. I felt like a good experiment would concentrate on reproducing just that weird phrasing.

Coincidentally, OpenAI had just released their new model, Astra, and I was looking for an excuse to kick its tires, so I decided to use it to run an experiment to see if I could reproduce any of the phenomena I’d been seeing. I couldn’t actually verify specifically that autoregression or attention were causing them, because those are internal to the LLM. But I felt like I could design an experiment that could provide some evidence, by structuring prompts in a way that would take advantage of how those mechanisms work. If I could get an AI to produce weird phrasing that showed some of the same problems as Yoda-speak, it would be evidence that these mechanisms were at least a potential root cause.

I used Astra as an orchestrator, and had it spin up a bunch of Luna sub-agents and give them almost identical prompts. Each consecutive sub-agent would get a small tweak in its prompt. I asked Astra to look at the output and see if there were any weird grammatical constructions that looked similar to Yoda-speak, then iterate on that prompt to make another small tweak, and keep going to produce increasingly weird output.

The first test was deliberately simple. Astra gave a fresh Luna writer this prompt:

Write one concise, natural paragraph that communicates every supplied fact. Use only the supplied facts. Do not pad the paragraph or repeat information to make it longer. Do not exceed 100 words. Do not mention these instructions, show a plan, use bullets, or explain your choices. Return only the paragraph.

Facts: The bicycle is blue. The bicycle has a narrow frame. The bicycle has a silver bell. The bicycle has a worn leather seat. The bicycle leans beside the garage. Rina rides the bicycle to work on weekdays. Rina locks the bicycle to the rack outside her office.

Luna turned that into a totally normal paragraph:

The blue bicycle has a narrow frame, a silver bell, and a worn leather seat. It leans beside the garage, and Rina rides it to work on weekdays, locking it to the rack outside her office.

Then Astra gave another fresh Luna writer exactly the same facts, with exactly the same wording, but changed their order. It moved the fact that the bicycle leans beside the garage and the fact that Rina rides it to work ahead of the color, frame, bell, and seat.

Luna mostly defeated the experiment. It had all of the facts before it started writing, and it was perfectly capable of moving them back where they belonged.

So Astra dropped the bicycle and wrote a fresh set of facts about something Luna had never seen, a completely made-up device with a steel slot called a “feed throat” that you push clay tiles through. It sent them with the same prompt as the bicycle:

Facts: The slot is made of steel. A clay tile slides through the slot. The slot is a hand’s width across. The slot is tapered. The slot is called the feed throat.

With no rule attached, Luna handled them the way it handled the bicycle:

The feed throat is a tapered steel slot, a hand’s width across, through which a clay tile slides.

Then Astra added two rules: the answer had to be one sentence, and it had to start with a fixed phrase. That phrase ends with the word slot, so everything else about the slot has to come after it.

The sentence must begin with exactly this text and continue from it:

Slide the clay tile through one more steel slot

Facts: The slot is a hand’s width across. The slot is tapered. The slot is called the feed throat.

Luna still tidied it up. Every time, it reached for a relative clause:

Slide the clay tile through one more steel slot, which is a hand’s width across, tapered, and called the feed throat.

Then Astra made one more small change. It kept the same opening and the same three facts, but wrote the facts as short pieces instead of complete sentences:

Facts: a hand’s width across tapered called the feed throat

And Luna wrote this:

Slide the clay tile through one more steel slot, a hand’s width across, tapered, called the feed throat.

The only thing that changed between those two runs was how the facts were written down. Astra tried the same setup on a completely different subject:

Rest the cracked bowl inside one more padded cradle, two palms wide, crescent-shaped, called the handling saddle.

That’s the sentence I’d been chasing. Once the model had committed to the noun and the remaining facts arrived as loose pieces instead of sentences, it tacked them on in the order they came.

The shape of its input, the model copies. Reorder the words it has already written, it cannot.

That still doesn’t tell me whether this is what happened when the model wrote one more small table, eight in and eight out, square, called the output projection. In these experiments, we deliberately pushed Luna into that kind of situation. In the original sentence, the model got there on its own.

I think the experiment shows that the model copies the shape of its input, and that fits my theory about the underlying attention and autoregression causes. When the three facts went in as complete sentences, Luna wrote a relative clause. The same facts sent in as bare fragments came back as bare fragments after the noun.

There are some obvious limitations to this experiment. I’m watching the model from the outside, so I don’t have any visibility into how the model weighted those tokens, or what its attention mechanism was doing. I also can’t say whether the model already had those three facts in mind when it wrote slot, but even if it did, it couldn’t put them anywhere but after the text it already generated. But the outputs match what those two mechanisms would do. Attention responds to how the prompt is written, as well as to what it says. Once the model has written the noun, it can’t go back and put anything in front of it.

I suspect that’s also why the AI keeps offering us that second answer. It can’t fix the Yoda-speak that it already generated. It can only write another sentence and hope that’s good enough.

item.title: When Architecture Decisions Actually Apply
item.dc:creator: Theo Valmis
item.description: In my previous Radar article, “Architectural Guardrails for AI-Generated Code,” I argued that AI coding agents need a layer that can hold architectural decisions in a structured corpus, retrieve the relevant ones, put them into the agent’s context before it writes code, and enforce explicit constraints with reproducible checks. Testing that model exposed two distinctions […]
item.content:encoded:
In my previous Radar article, “Architectural Guardrails for AI-Generated Code,” I argued that AI coding agents need a layer that can hold architectural decisions in a structured corpus, retrieve the relevant ones, put them into the agent’s context before it writes code, and enforce explicit constraints with reproducible checks. Testing that model exposed two distinctions I had compressed together.

  1. Retrieving a decision because it is relevant doesn’t mean the decision applies to the artifact being changed.
  2. A decision that does apply isn’t automatically suitable for deterministic enforcement.

The first distinction is between relevance and authority; the second is between guidance and enforcement.

Here’s the story of how one controlled repository made this distinction clear. The project used local JSON-backed persistence for its current phase, and an active architecture decision ruled out PostgreSQL, ORMs, and database migrations for the command-line application. The task asked the coding agent to change that application’s storage module, so the decision was not merely related to persistence in general; it had authority over the part of the repository being changed. The record was retrieved successfully and placed in the agent’s context before work began.

The agent still proposed PostgreSQL, together with an ORM and a migration path. Under my original four-capability model, that looked at first like a retrieval failure. It wasn’t. The decision was found and was current, and it arrived at the right moment. What was missing was an applicability signal that told the system that this decision governed the storage module being edited rather than serving as one more relevant document for the model to weigh against nearby code and other context.

Retrieval finds; applicability governs

Retrieval helps us determine which architectural decisions might be relevant to a task. That’s a search problem, and teams have increasingly capable ways to solve it: indexed repositories, connected documentation, exposed decision records and service catalogs, semantic search, and project memory. These techniques help an agent see useful material before it writes code. They don’t, by themselves, answer a different question: Which of those decisions has authority over the change in front of the agent?

Suppose a repository contains two persistence decisions. One requires PostgreSQL for an analytics service; the other requires local file storage for a command-line tool. If the agent is editing the command-line tool’s storage module, both decisions may rank highly for a query about persistence, but only the local-storage decision applies to that artifact. Determining which decision governs the change requires scope, lifecycle, precedence, and a clear record of which decisions replace earlier ones. I argued for precedence and lifecycle in the previous article; scope deserves equal attention because scope is what tells the system where a decision has authority.

A related problem is that architectural information is usually scattered across several kinds of documents. Humans know that an old design note, a README, an accepted architecture decision record, and a current platform standard don’t necessarily carry the same authority, even when all four discuss the same topic. Models don’t know that unless the system preserves the distinction. When those sources are flattened into one context window, the hierarchy among them can disappear. I think of this as authority flattening: Information remains available, but the signal about which information is binding becomes weaker. That’s useful when a design question is genuinely open; it’s risky when the team has already answered the question.

Research on architectural decision violations points to a similar boundary. A 2026 study by Su and colleagues examined 980 ADRs across 109 open source repositories. The models were strong when decisions were explicit and inferable from code but less accurate when compliance depended on deployment configuration or organizational knowledge. The study evaluated violations after code was written rather than guidance before generation, but the underlying limitation is similar: A model can retrieve the right document and still make the wrong architectural choice when applicability or authority remains implicit.

What scope changed

I tested this distinction in a small controlled experiment using seven coding tasks, repeated under two conditions with the same coding agent and model configuration. In one condition the agent worked without the relevant architectural guidance; in the other, architectural decisions were supplied before it began changing code. Independent reviewers assessed the first attempts for both architectural compliance and whether the requested work was actually completed. The guidance changed behavior: First-attempt compliance on the architecture-sensitive tasks improved from 6 of 15 runs to 10 of 15, while successful task completion was essentially unchanged.

The more interesting result was a failure inside the guided condition. In several authentication tasks, the agent received a storage-related architectural decision that was genuinely relevant to the surrounding problem and then implemented additional persistence work that the task had never asked for. Nothing was wrong with the decision, and retrieval had done its job. Relevance had simply been presented without enough information about authority. The experiment made two limits explicit: A decision can be relevant without governing the artifact being changed, and even a governing decision doesn’t authorize the agent to widen the task. Applicability tells the system where a decision may constrain work; it isn’t permission to invent more work.

Blocking is easier than guiding

The second distinction forced me to revise another part of the original model. The previous article emphasized deterministic enforcement: when a team has made an explicit decision and a violation can be identified from observable evidence, a blocking verdict should come from a reproducible rule rather than a model’s judgment. I still think that’s the right standard for blocking. The important qualification is that only a subset of architectural decisions can meet it without pretending that judgment has become deterministic.

“Do not introduce SQLAlchemy into this component” is comparatively easy to express as a rule, easy to check, and easy to block. “Use the existing persistence abstraction correctly” is different. Most of its meaning is architectural rather than syntactic: The right implementation depends on which abstraction is intended, how it’s used in this part of the system, and what surrounding constraints are already in force. The first statement describes a prohibition that can plausibly become a deterministic control. The second describes a sanctioned path and is better treated as guidance unless the team can make the relevant evidence and boundary precise.

Earlier experiments with pregeneration guidance pointed in the same direction. Adding more architecture-related context didn’t reliably improve behavior because what was missing was often not another prohibition; it was a clearer description of the accepted implementation path. A guardrail layer built entirely around blocking will become very good at saying no. Useful architectural governance has to do both jobs: block the known violations when the evidence is precise enough and carry positive architectural direction for the much larger set of decisions that still require interpretation.

When judgment becomes authority

This doesn’t reduce the role of models; it puts probabilistic reasoning where it’s useful. Models are good at interpretation: reading ambiguous guidance, surfacing decisions that might bear on a change, explaining the consequences of a boundary violation, and proposing how to bring a change back into line with the intended design. Deterministic logic is better suited to decisions the team has already settled and can state in terms that a check can reproduce. The mistake is asking either mechanism to do both jobs.

Once a system says that a proposed change violates an architectural rule, the standard changes. An engineer should be able to ask which decision applied, why it applied to this part of the codebase, what evidence triggered the result, and whether another developer running the same check would get the same answer. That doesn’t require every part of architecture to become formal policy. It requires a clear boundary around where uncertainty is allowed: Models may help find and explain architectural context, but a blocking decision shouldn’t ultimately reduce to “the model thought this looked wrong.”

Humans routinely work with architectural ambiguity. We weigh incomplete evidence, local context, and competing trade-offs, often using heuristics rather than formal rules. Models can help with that interpretive work too, but the result remains probabilistic. The problem begins when an ambiguous judgment is treated as a blocking rule. Deterministic enforcement requires a boundary precise enough that the same evidence produces the same verdict.

The distinction matters even more when a team uses several coding tools at once. One developer may use Claude Code, another Codex, another Cursor, while automated agents perform background maintenance. The models and retrieval mechanisms can differ, but the team’s architecture shouldn’t change with the tool. A shared set of decisions can sit underneath those environments as the source of authority, while each tool consumes guidance in its own way and the enforceable subset is checked consistently.

What I would add to the original model

I would now amend the original four-capability model in two places.

Retrieval should surface candidate decisions, while applicability determines which of those decisions actually govern the current artifact or action, using scope together with lifecycle and precedence. Then guidance and enforcement should remain separate outcomes: Some applicable decisions are precise enough to support deterministic controls, while others should influence the implementation without becoming binary rules.

That separation leaves the agent free to reason where the architecture is genuinely open while preserving authority where the team has already made a decision. It also avoids a common overcorrection. Once teams see that some architecture can be enforced automatically, the temptation is to formalize everything. A great deal of architecture is still judgment. “Keep domain boundaries narrow” or “prefer asynchronous integration when immediate consistency is unnecessary” can be valuable guidance without being safe material for an automatic block. The level of authority a system exercises should follow the precision of the decision and the evidence available to evaluate it.

For years architectural governance ran largely on human process: Someone wrote the decision record, an architect reviewed the important changes, experienced engineers carried part of the history in their heads, and code review caught some of what slipped through. AI coding agents change the economics of that process because implementation can now move faster than architectural intent can be reexplained and rereviewed by hand. Giving agents more context is necessary, but it’s not sufficient. The harder job is preserving the difference between information that may be useful, a decision that actually applies, guidance that should shape an implementation, and a constraint that is precise enough to stop one.

The goal isn’t to constrain every choice an agent makes. It’s to stop decisions the team has already made from quietly turning back into suggestions. That requires more than retrieving the right document. The system has to know whether the decision is current, where it has authority, and what kind of authority the team intended it to have.

item.description: In the final episode of Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes, AI engineer Sajal Sharma showed how to build a personal assistant on OpenClaw that tracks your tasks and notes and handles scheduled work on its own. A useful personal assistant has to be reachable when you’re away from your computer and keep running when […]
item.content:encoded:
In the final episode of Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes, AI engineer Sajal Sharma showed how to build a personal assistant on OpenClaw that tracks your tasks and notes and handles scheduled work on its own.

A useful personal assistant has to be reachable when you’re away from your computer and keep running when it has scheduled work to do. OpenClaw supports both, and you decide where the agent runs, which models it uses, and how it accesses your data.

How to go from a fresh install to scheduled automations, step-by-step

  1. Install your OpenClaw instance. Sajal recommends starting locally while you learn how it works, then moving to an always-on machine or hosted environment if you need continuous availability.
  2. Connect the channels you use. Add a messaging channel such as Telegram, WhatsApp, or Slack so you can reach the assistant away from your desk. Sajal used Telegram in his demo to send requests and receive notifications from the same assistant.
  3. Set up the assistant’s workspace. Give the agent a place to keep tasks, notes, skills, and memory, along with guidance files that define how it behaves and how it should work with the files in that workspace.
  4. Use it in your daily workflows. Sajal asked the assistant for an overview of current projects and checked progress toward a reading goal. He also had it search the web for a book series and add the books it found to his reading list.
  5. Add proactive automations. Schedule work the assistant should handle on its own. Sajal added a Telegram reminder and a morning briefing designed to pull from tasks, a calendar, and recent email. Recurring checks and webhooks can also trigger the agent when something changes in another system.

Thanks for following Zero to Agent

This episode closes out Zero to Agent in 30 Minutes. Thanks for watching and building along with our presenters throughout the series.

If you’d like to keep following how agents can take on more complex work, tune in to The Monday Morning Agent, which debuts Monday, October 12, at 8am PT/11am ET. The eight-episode series follows the development of an increasingly autonomous data agent working with real play-by-play data. Learn more and save your seat or follow along here on Radar.

item.title: Designing Websites for People and AI Agents with WebMCP
item.dc:creator: Angie Jones
item.description: The following article originally appeared on the Agentic AI Foundation blog and is being reposted here with the author’s permission. Websites are designed for people. We can look at a page and quickly understand where to enter information or which control will complete an action. AI agents don’t see or use the web the same […]
item.content:encoded:
The following article originally appeared on the Agentic AI Foundation blog and is being reposted here with the author’s permission.

Websites are designed for people. We can look at a page and quickly understand where to enter information or which control will complete an action.

AI agents don’t see or use the web the same way we do. An agent may have to process a screenshot or inspect the page’s underlying structure, then reason about which control matches the request.

The additional context increases token use, and each interpretation step creates another chance for error.

WebMCP (not to be confused with MCP) gives web developers a standard way to publish structured tools to access the capabilities of their website enabling agents to call those functions with structured inputs.

A developer can register a tool through document.modelContext and give it a name and description. The tool also defines an input schema and the function that runs when an agent calls it.

For example, an article site could publish a search tool that calls the same application code as its visible search form.

const searchToolController = new AbortController();

await document.modelContext.registerTool(
  {
    name: "search-articles",
    title: "Search articles",
    description: "Search published articles by topic.",
    inputSchema: {
      type: "object",
      properties: {
        query: {
          type: "string",
          description: "The topic or phrase to search for."
        }
      },
      required: ["query"],
      additionalProperties: false
    },
    async execute({ query }) {
      const articles = await searchArticles(query);
      renderSearchResults(articles);
      return { articles };
    }
  },
  { signal: searchToolController.signal }
);

// Call this when the search tool should no longer be available.
// searchToolController.abort();

The name and description tell the agent when to use the tool. The input schema defines the arguments it can send. The execute function calls the site’s existing search logic and updates the page with the results.

The browser makes the registered tool available to a supported agent while the page is active. When the agent calls it, the browser passes the structured arguments to execute and returns the result.

When the search tool should no longer be available, the page can unregister it by calling searchToolController.abort().

A page registers tools that match its current state. A content view may provide a search tool, while an editor can provide tools for changing the selected content. The agent then discovers the tools available for the page’s current state.

WebMCP also proposes a declarative path for existing HTML forms. The article search could be exposed through attributes on the form itself.

<form
  action="/articles"
  method="get"
  toolname="search-articles"
  tooldescription="Search published articles by topic."
>
  <label for="article-query">Topic</label>
  <input
    id="article-query"
    name="query"
    type="search"
    toolparamdescription="The topic or phrase to search for."
    required
  >
  <button type="submit">Search</button>
</form>

The browser uses the form attributes and controls to create the tool definition. Because the form omits toolautosubmit, the browser populates the field but leaves the final click to the person. The person can review the search query and click the Search button.

Keep the person and agent in the same interface

A WebMCP tool uses the state already visible in the application and the person’s active session. The shared page gives the person a place to review the agent’s work. When the agent completes an action, the person can see the updated state and make changes through the normal interface.

Web developers can also reuse application logic that already handles the visible interface. OpenAI’s Runme example is a browser application that registers tools for reading instructions and updating notebook content. Runme can offer those functions through the page without adding a separate server only to expose an MCP endpoint.

Pair WebMCP with MCP

WebMCP and MCP both expose tools to agents, but they operate in different parts of an application. Understanding the difference helps developers decide where each one fits and how they can work together.

An MCP server can provide tools when no related page is open. A WebMCP tool is attached to the current document and can use the page’s current state.

WebMCP standardizes how a page registers tools with the browser. The browser can present those tools to its agent through MCP or another function calling mechanism.

MCP Apps address another part of the interaction. An MCP server can provide an interactive interface that a compatible host displays to a person. WebMCP lets an agent use functions from an existing website.

WebMCP and MCP Apps can work together. For example, a shopping website could publish a compare_products tool through WebMCP. An MCP server could provide an MCP App for the comparison, so the person can adjust the options while the agent handles the supporting work.

The comparison interface could also be described with A2UI, which lets an agent describe an interface in a declarative format. The client renders the description with components from its own design system, so the client controls which components are available and how they behave.

People and agents can use the same interface at the same time. Developers need to decide which functions the agent can call and what the person should see while those functions run.

Design the page for agent use

Agent use begins before the first click. An agent may need to discover the website and determine how to authenticate. It may choose an API or structured documentation before opening a browser.

Web teams should study how agents use their site before deciding which interface to add. Check the server logs to see whether agents are crawling HTML or requesting machine readable content. Tool activity can reveal which WebMCP functions agents discover and which calls they abandon.

Keep existing controls in the execution path

WebMCP reduces the amount of interface interpretation an agent has to do, but a structured tool is still an entry point into the application. The website should apply its existing access controls and input validation whenever the tool runs.

For example, an update_cart tool can accept a product identifier and quantity. The server should confirm that the product exists and that the current user can modify the cart. Structured input doesn’t automatically make the request trusted, so the server should run the same checks it uses for updates made through the website.

The browser also has a responsibility. OpenAI reviews each site tool call before it runs and asks the person to confirm sensitive actions. The WebMCP draft requires origin isolation, and its tools permissions policy allows same origin use by default.

Clients need to handle tool changes during a task. A page can change a tool’s identity or schema after the agent begins working, so the client should review the tool again before using the new definition.

Researchers are already testing those boundaries. A June preprint on WebMCP tool surface poisoning found that changes to tool registration and metadata could redirect agents in its test environment. The researchers used a polyfill and a headless agent, so a native browser implementation may behave differently. But these reported attacks can serve as great test cases as you’re adding WebMCP to your site.

Test WebMCP while the design is open

WebMCP already has several experimental implementations. Chrome offers an implementation through a flag and an origin trial. Sarah Drasner created an interactive WebMCP demo of this implementation that you can try in your browser.

Cloudflare released a developer preview that can add a WebMCP bridge to a website, and Brave has tested WebMCP with its Leo assistant.

Testing WebMCP against varied applications can reveal assumptions in the current draft. For example, a form may need a declarative feature that has not been specified yet. Also, look for lifecycle problems when a website changes its tools during a task.

Bring your findings back to the WebMCP issue tracker.

item.content:encoded:
AI systems are gaining more autonomy while governments, companies, and researchers are still working out how much oversight they need. On the latest episode of This Week in AI, we covered the US debate over AI governance, new frontier models, persistent agents, world models, and practical uses for AI in healthcare and disaster response.

AI oversight is moving beyond company promises

The Trump administration announced a voluntary agreement with major AI companies that calls for internal safety monitoring, external audits, and independent board reviews. Because the agreement carries no legal enforcement, it raises a familiar question about how far self-regulation can go when companies are developing increasingly powerful systems.

Government agencies are also testing what existing law can do. The Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI companies focused on potential consumer risks. Cases like these could help establish whether current consumer protection laws are enough or whether AI will require a more specialized regulatory framework.

For technical leaders, regulation can influence how organizations evaluate models, document risks, manage access, and choose vendors. As AI moves deeper into business processes, teams will need governance practices that can withstand outside review.

AI systems are taking on longer, more autonomous work

OpenAI just released Dots, its “proactive assistant” designed to retain context, work across applications, pursue multiple goals, and act independently. To do that work without waiting for a prompt, Dots needs standing access to the apps and data it works across. That also increases the amount of personal data an agent can reach and raises the cost of mistakes or misuse.

Google is also extending how long a model can work on a task. The company says Gemini 4 Argon can generate up to a million output tokens in a single response, far beyond the typical output limits of current frontier models. The goal is to let a model stay with long multistep work such as extensive coding or financial and legal analysis. Longer-running models and persistent agents aren’t the same thing, but both let AI finish more work without handing control back to a person.

As agents act more on their own, they need to anticipate the consequences of their actions. That becomes even more important when AI moves beyond software and begins acting in the physical world. World models aim to teach AI how these environments work, including cause and effect, which is why many researchers see them as building blocks for robotics and physical AI. World Labs (recently acquired by AMD) is developing spatial intelligence models for interactive 3D environments, while British startup Worldmodeldata has licensed nearly 1 million hours of video game data paired with player actions. Researchers from NVIDIA, MIT, and Oxford also introduced Physis-Lang, which uses descriptions of physical causes and effects to help video models learn why events happen. Researchers still don’t know which training approach will work best, so they’re testing several kinds of data and model design.

AI support experts in high-stakes work

Anthropic’s Claude is helping teams responding to an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo organize daily reports, compare forecasting models, analyze genomic information, and support vaccine research. Researchers have also developed a Spanish-language speech model that may eventually help identify accelerated biological aging and early signs of dementia. Mayo Clinic researchers built a model that identifies patterns associated with elevated pancreatic cancer risk years before diagnosis. Following severe flooding in Nepal, local teams used AI to match reports of missing people with victim lists and map damaged buildings using satellite imagery.

Together, these examples show how AI can be used for good by helping people work through complex information faster and, ultimately, save lives, while keeping qualified experts responsible for the final decisions.

What’s next

As AI takes on more work and enters higher-stakes settings, organizations will need clearer answers about access and accountability. They’ll also need to decide where human judgment remains necessary as systems become more capable.

Join us again next Monday for another episode of This Week in AI, when we’ll dive into more of the news, issues, and key developments shaping the AI era. And check back each Friday for the latest episode, or watch on YouTube, Spotify, Apple, or wherever you get your podcasts.

item.dc:creator: Vicki Reyzelman
item.custom:subtitle: The web is building an identity layer for AI agents. It will tell you who’s knocking. It won’t tell you whether to open the door.
item.description: On a recent episode of This Week in AI, we discussed that the number of nonhumans on the internet is greater than humans, 144 to 1. It’s an estimate, and the order of magnitude is more important than the number itself. What matters is what a ratio anywhere in that range does to a security […]
item.content:encoded:
On a recent episode of This Week in AI, we discussed that the number of nonhumans on the internet is greater than humans, 144 to 1. It’s an estimate, and the order of magnitude is more important than the number itself. What matters is what a ratio anywhere in that range does to a security architecture. For more than two decades, systems were engineered around two foundational assumptions: either verifying a human user exercising discretionary judgment or validating the account executing hardcoded predictable logic. Autonomous AI agents shatter both sides of this legacy identity taxonomy because they possess broad, human-like operational scope across multiple internal and external applications while remaining inherently nondeterministic and probabilistic in their reasoning.

Today, because the agent is interacting on behalf of a human through a genuine browser with standard extensions, its technical fingerprint looks identical to a normal human user’s device. Agents call tools, observe results, and revise. A person browses, hands off to an agent, and takes the session back. All the activity appears to be coming from the same user.

Signed agents help the identity problem, and they’re arriving. Web Bot Auth is a thin layer over RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures where an agent declares its identity and purpose. But they only help with the identity problem: The signature proves who is making the request, not the intent behind it. Prompt injection and other techniques can be used to steer a verified, well-behaved agent into acting against your interest without its operator ever knowing.

The organizations getting this right are treating agent policy as a commercial question with a security implementation. The following questions need to be answered:

  • Which agents do we allow to use our service?
  • What endpoints do we need to protect? 
  • How will agent management security policies impact revenue?

Here are the techniques successful companies are using to secure in the agentic era. A phased strategic roadmap implementing continuous execution-time verification. These are the steps:

  1. Establish execution-time machine identity and scoped delegation. Replace static, long-lived API keys with machine single sign-on mechanisms that issue short-lived, context-bound credentials at the time of tool execution. Enforce strict delegation policies so that autonomous agents operate within verified “green zones” without inheriting broad human privileges.
  2. Deploy cryptographic ingress verification. Upgrade edge infrastructure to inspect Web Bot Auth HTTP Message Signatures, in order to separate cryptographically verified crawlers from anonymous traffic.
  3. Upgrade edge defenses to browser-layer intent classification. Transition legacy network-layer antibot web application firewall (WAF) to client-side browser-layer detection platforms. 
  4. Harden agent execution pipelines against prompt injection. Instrument robust input sanitization, instruction hierarchy enforcement, and design-level safeguards around all LLM ingestion channels to neutralize indirect prompt injection attacks before external web content reaches execution tools.
  5. Adopt standardization for agentic commerce and admission. Integrate emerging trust frameworks such as the Framework for Agentic Commerce Trust (FACT), a neutral real-time trust layer for AI-driven transactions in addition to verification protocols like CAPTCHA to validate agentic capability vectors before delegating sensitive interagent tasks.

The rapid transition from human-directed software to autonomous AI agents breaks traditional enterprise security paradigms. AI agents operate with broad operational scope but nondeterministic, probabilistic reasoning. This is causing static perimeter defenses to fail. The teams that come through this well will be the ones that stopped asking “Who’s on the other end of the connection?” and started asking “What’s this request for, and what happens if it succeeds?”

item.title: The Preservation Gap in the AI Stack: Why Capability Is Advancing Faster Than Reconstructability
item.dc:creator: Monika Dvorackova
item.description: Artificial intelligence systems are difficult to reproduce because their behavior depends on nondeterministic models and on data, configurations, policies, and external services that continue to change.
